item.title: UK man accused of planning terrorism acts against Nigel Farage also charged in murder of another politician
item.description: A man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe faces terrorism charges involving an alleged plot against Nigel Farage.
item.content:encoded:
British prosecutors announced terrorism charges Friday against a 28-year-old man already in custody for the murder of a conservative politician.

The Crown Prosecution Service charged Joshua Kerry of South Yorkshire with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, accusing him of "engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism, including against [Reform UK leader] Nigel Farage MP." 

Kerry has been in the custody of His Majesty's government since late July, after he was arrested and accused of murdering former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe.

Prosecutors say Widdecombe was eating lunch in her Devon home on July 8, when Kerry allegedly walked through the front door, beat her 21 times in the head with a hammer, took her wallet and was gone in an attack that lasted only two minutes.

Authorities say the latest charges against Kerry are related to events that took place between May 31 and July 8. 

In a statement, Senior National Coordinator for Counterterrorism Policing, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, said: "The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counterterrorism Policing network. This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of inquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge."

UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, posting on X, called the new charges against Kerry "extremely concerning" and sent her "profound sympathies" to the Farage family. She added that "an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all. This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life." 

IRAN PROBED IN ALLEGED TERRORISM PLOT AT UK BASE

The Jo Cox Foundation, set up in honor of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016, said in a statement, "No one in public life should have to fear for their safety. Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endangered individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life. We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics."

Kerry is due back at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.

Separately on Friday, Counterterrorism Policing also announced charges against two Iranian men accused of plotting "to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area." 

The Crown Prosecution Service charged 36-year-old Salam Ahmadyan and 34-year-old Rahman Salehi with "engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts, contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006," alleging that two men were "in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot."  

SUSPECT CHARGED IN MURDER OF UK POLITICIAN ANNE WIDDECOMBE

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Evans called the charges "extremely serious" while reiterating that "we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter." 

Evans noted the alleged plot comes during the High Holy Day period and "coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing anti-Semitic incidents across the UK."

Ahmadyan and Salehi have been remanded and are set to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Saturday.

Fox News’ Thomas Ferraro and Stephanie Bennett and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: JUAN WILLIAMS: My wife thought I was crazy to join Fox News. I'm glad I did
item.description: Juan Williams reflects on leaving CNN to join Rupert Murdoch's startup Fox News Channel 30 years ago and the friendships that defined his career.
item.content:encoded:
My wife said I was crazy.

This was 1996, thirty years ago.

I worked for the established brand name in cable television, CNN.

FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER

Why then, she asked, with three young school-age children still at home, was I willing to give up that prime seat to join a start-up cable network being launched by a controversial Australian media mogul, Rupert Murdoch?

And this start-up Fox News Channel faced an uphill fight just to get on cable systems in big cities, including New York.

"Crazy!" Yes! But I told her they were going to be scrappy, innovative, and give me a foothold on the ground floor of the next era of news.

So, I went with the new kids in cable news.

And Fox delivered over the last 30 years by doing news for people who did not watch news. Fox is now often the number one channel of any kind on cable.

From the early days, the screen has been full of colorful graphics. Stories come and go fast. Heroes and villains are clear-cut. Crime stories and war stories took center stage — no matter where they occurred.

The on-air people did not speak down to the audience as experts. They talked to them as friends and neighbors, always shaking their heads at a crazy world.

As Brit Hume, now Fox's chief political analyst, told me at the start, Fox was willing to do stories being ignored by the news networks and cable outlets. He said Fox News was picking up money others left on the street.

DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE

On top of being daring, Fox had the novel idea of featuring right-of-center voices, Republican political players who generally felt like outsiders on the other networks.

Roger Ailes, the first head of the network, knew politics. He was a top GOP consultant. And his top programming aide, Chet Collier, a Democrat, had been Ailes' mentor at the popular daytime talk show, "The Mike Douglas Show."

They sold me on Fox, and they knew exactly what they were getting with me. I'd worked at The Washington Post and CNN. In bestselling books, I called out politicians on the right and the left.

And as a Black journalist, I was known to trade punches with Black politicians.

Fox's founders wanted me to trade punches with their right-wing media personalities. I was happy to get in on the action.

From the start, Fox made good television. Ratings slowly climbed as viewers discovered turn-up-the-volume debates among finger-pointing, smirking, laughing, and eye-rolling personalities.

Fox was in the right place as bombshell revelations hit the air about the president of the United States having a sexual relationship with a White House intern.

DR. MARC SIEGEL: WHAT 18 YEARS AT FOX TAUGHT ME ABOUT COURAGE AND FAITH

The impeachment of a president included nightly stories about the popular President Clinton facing a hard-edged prosecutor, Kenneth Starr. And then came provocative reports about a blue dress and cigars. The ratings climbed.

What I remember most about those early years of Fox is being on set in the D.C. bureau with Brit Hume, then the managing editor. He held the air for hours of hearings and press conferences. I was by his side as we struggled with new equipment, technicians discovering buttons, and producers shouting breaking news into our earpieces.

The same chaos followed when "Fox News Sunday" hit the air. No studio was ready. So, Tony Snow, the show's first moderator, and Marty Ryan, the top producer, had to hunt for historic homes, even gardens, in Washington, D.C.

For Snow, Hume, and an all-star panel of D.C. commentators, including Fred Barnes, Mort Kondracke — hail to the Beltway Boys — Mara Liasson, Bill Kristol, and Charles Krauthammer, every show was about speaking directly to the hot, populist passions in politics.

It was about being sharp with each other and giving no quarter to political guests. Creating the best show for the people at home has remained the goal for Fox.

Krauthammer would win laughs and applause on the lecture circuit by beginning his speeches by saying he was grateful to be invited anywhere Juan Williams could not interrupt him.

By 2000, Fox was perfectly positioned to offer 24/7 news and analysis of the disputed presidential election, the Florida recount, and the 5–4 Supreme Court decision that gave the White House to an underdog Republican who lost the popular vote.

And when terrorists struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001 — 25 years ago this month — Fox was there with an established news-gathering operation and unique access to the new Republican administration of President George W. Bush. Then came Fox News' coverage of the war in Iraq and the fight against terrorist cells in Afghanistan.

Fox's ratings grew as more and more viewers trusted that, no matter their politics, Fox delivered the most compelling take on the sizzling stories defining each election, especially the 2008 race that saw a little-known Black senator running against former First Lady Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination.

GREGG JARRETT: MY MOTHER’S ADVICE LED ME TO THE CAREER OF A LIFETIME

It was a freezing night in Des Moines when the "All-Star" panel realized Barack Obama, a Black man, was about to win the Iowa caucuses.

On the air, I started crying. My emotion got to me as I tried to explain to the Fox audience what that moment meant to our nation's history, and especially to Black American history.

Another memory is being lustily booed by an auditorium full of South Carolina Republican voters in 2012. The booing started when, while asking questions at a Fox-sponsored GOP primary debate, I questioned Newt Gingrich about his use of racially loaded rhetoric concerning President Obama and the poor.

Years later, I would joke with the Speaker that he had me to thank for his upset victory in the Palmetto State primary.

That exchange became one of the first viral moments of a presidential campaign in the early internet age.

FOX NEWS DIGITAL LEADS IN UNIQUE VISITORS, OTHER KEY METRICS AGAINST CNN, NY TIMES DURING AUGUST

By Obama's second term, I was spending more time in the New York studios as a co-host of "The Five." By 2015, I began nearly a decade of living in New York to co-host the show. My role was described by Ailes as a center-left foil to the conservatives on the show.

Politico summed up my role this way: "Fox's Lone-Wolf Liberal Had a Tough Job. But It Made for Better TV."

"Juan Williams was particularly good at what might be the hardest, least appreciated, and most important job in cable news," the outlet wrote.

"The Five" became the number one show on the number one cable channel and delivered a robust message about debate in America. No matter your politics, no matter if you are with conservatives or liberals, and no matter racial and religious lines, "We the People" — Americans of all stripes — can find common ground in defense of honest debate, even with rants and occasional posturing.

"You cut a path through the jungle," a friend recently told me as we reminisced about the state of the media and the dearth today of conservative media platforms where liberals feel comfortable appearing, as well as liberal platforms where conservatives feel comfortable appearing.

I told him that since Fox became the number one cable news channel, it is often the case that more Democrats are watching Fox than any other cable news channel.

I've written more than a dozen books over the last 30 years. And on book tours, hard-right conservatives show up to tell me they disagree with me but love hearing a different point of view from someone they trust and, sometimes grudgingly, even like.

In truth, working with Brit, Shannon Bream, Bret Baier, Bill O'Reilly, Sean Hannity, and so many others almost always ended with more conversation, then dinner, a ballgame, or a beer. Brit once said the two of us are like TV's pro wrestlers. We fight like hell tonight, and the next night we go to another town and do it again.

At its best, Fox News is a reminder that social media and the internet are not real life. The bitterness we see online is produced by computer algorithms designed to divide Americans. Fox is about the audience. There's a bond.

That is why, on Fox News' 30th anniversary, I find myself thinking less about ratings or political fights than about friendships.

I think about Charles.

I think about Tony.

I think about Roger and Chet.

I think about Brit, Mara, Bill, Fred, Chris, and Bret.

I think about people like Cherie Grzech, who directed politics, and Porter Berry, who ran shows before taking control of FoxNews.com. I think about former television producer Nate Fredman. I think about Lynne Jordal Martin, who edits for FoxNews.com. I shared offices with Mike Emanuel and Leland Vittert.

I think about the amazing Fox audience — the countless people who treat me as a friend when we meet in diners, airports, supermarkets, campaign rallies, ball games, convention halls, studios, and green rooms across America.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And I think about the people viewers rarely see: editors, producers, bookers, tech operators, directors, hair and makeup artists, security guards, and janitors.

So, three cheers for Fox News — one for each decade we have been on the air.

Thank you to the viewers and FoxNews.com readers who made our success possible.

Thirty years ago, my wife thought I was crazy.

She still thinks I am, and maybe she's right.

But I'm awfully glad I took the chance.

item.title: Karine Jean-Pierre admits Biden admin failed on economic, age messaging, but claims Trump making same mistake
item.description: Karine Jean-Pierre argued President Donald Trump is repeating former President Joe Biden's messaging failures on the economy, warning that grocery and gas prices remain undefeated.
item.content:encoded:
Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre argued in an opinion piece published Friday that President Donald Trump was making the same messaging mistakes as her former boss, former President Joe Biden.

"Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda," she wrote in The New York Times guest essay. "His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land. Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation."

Jean-Pierre pointed to the president's messaging on gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran in the piece, and said, "When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses."

"The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging," she wrote.

FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH

When asked about Jean-Pierre's argument, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Biden’s policies destroyed our economy by creating the worst inflation crisis in history, instituting burdensome red tape, and stifling American energy dominance. 

"President Trump has fixed the disaster that Joe Biden created by cooling inflation, signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering drug prices, and reshoring our manufacturing industry. The fake news won’t, so President Trump will continue to tout his economic wins to Americans."

Jean-Pierre admitted the administration misread the public and said her press briefings fueled much of the debate surrounding Biden's age, in addition to the economic messaging.

"We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it," she conceded.

TRUMP VS HISTORY: HOW PRESIDENT'S POLL NUMBERS COMPARE TO BIDEN, OBAMA, BUSH AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

She also pointed to the changing media ecosystem and said, "A TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump," would get more attention than her press briefings or a cabinet official on the Sunday news programs.

"The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds," Jean-Pierre wrote. "His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated."

"Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now," she concluded.

KAROLINE LEAVITT REVEALS SHE’S ADVISED TRUMP ON WHITE HOUSE REPLACEMENT IN FINAL INTERVIEW AS PRESS SECRETARY

Jean-Pierre released a book in 2025 about her time in the White House titled, "Independent."

Ahead of its release, she revealed that she was leaving the Democratic Party and registering as an Independent.

"The Democratic Party had defined my life, my career," Jean-Pierre wrote. "Everything I’d done to make people’s lives better had been connected to it. The party was the vehicle that allowed me not just to have a front seat to history, working first on [Barack] Obama’s presidential campaign then in his administration, but also to make some history of my own as the first Black woman and openly queer person to ever be a White House press secretary. Never had I considered leaving the party until now."

item.title: FOX News Media tops YouTube for eighth straight quarter with 918 million views
item.description: FOX News Media hit 918 million YouTube views in the third quarter of 2026, outpacing MS NOW, CNN, ABC News, NBC News and CBS News once again.
item.content:encoded:
FOX News Media closed out the third quarter of 2026 as the No. 1 news brand on YouTube for the eighth consecutive quarter, and the company continues to dominate across multiple platforms.

During the news-heavy quarter, Fox News piled up 918 million video views to lead all competitors. MS NOW finished with 889 million, CNN managed 712 million, ABC delivered 442 million, NBC News secured 356 million and CBS News settled for 149 million video views, according to Emplifi.

Fox News has garnered 3.5 billion video views in 2026 to lead its nearest competitor, MS NOW, by 32%.

'THE FIVE' LEADS CABLE NEWS FOR 20TH STRAIGHT QUARTER AS FOX NEWS OUTDRAWS CNN AND MS NOW COMBINED

During the third quarter, FOX Business’ YouTube generated 139 million video views to lead business competition for the 27th consecutive quarter, according to Comscore Social.

The YouTube success comes as Fox News Channel topped all of cable during the third quarter, crushing CNN and MS NOW combined in multiple categories.

Fox News also ranked No. 1 in social engagement with 280 million social media interactions across Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok, according to Emplifi.

Fox News had 85.1 million Facebook interactions, 54.1 million Instagram interactions, 14.6 million X interactions and 126.7 million TikTok interactions.

item.title: Crime, kidnappings and drone attacks flagged in US warning for border region
item.description: The U.S. Embassy flagged drone attacks near the Colombia-Venezuela border, urging Americans to avoid Norte de Santander due to kidnapping and conflict.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. officials are warning Americans to stay away from a region of Latin America amid an elevated threat of attacks by armed groups using explosive-rigged drones.

The U.S. Embassy in Colombia posted the warning about Colombia's Norte de Santander Department, also known as North Santander, Sept. 29.

Norte de Santander Department is located in northeastern Colombia along the country's border with Venezuela.

TERRORISM, ARMED CONFLICT PROMPT STARK WARNING FOR AMERICANS VISITING SCENIC SPOT

Americans are urged not to travel to the area — or within 5 miles of the Colombia-Venezuela border — due to crime, kidnapping and conflict between armed groups.

U.S. citizens are also urged to reconsider travel to all other regions of Colombia, according to State Department guidance in recent months.

The area faces an "elevated risk of attacks" from illegal armed groups in the Norte de Santander Department, according to the embassy's Sept. 29 statement.

This includes the National Liberation Army (ELN), which the U.S. designates as a foreign terrorist organization (FTO).

‘DO NOT PHYSICALLY RESIST’: US ISSUES CHILLING ROBBERY WARNING FOR AMERICANS OVERSEAS

"Groups in the Catatumbo region have repeatedly used commercially available drones fitted with explosives, often combined with rifle fire, to attack police substations and military installations," the statement said.

Officials also warned that the groups "may conduct attacks with little or no warning against police stations, government buildings, military installations and related infrastructure in Norte de Santander Department."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Embassy officials advised Americans to keep a low profile and "be aware of your surroundings at all times."

"Exercise heightened vigilance, particularly near police stations, government buildings, military installations and along major roads," the statement said. 

"Do not confront armed individuals."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Americans are also urged to avoid crowds and demonstrations and to monitor local media for security updates.

Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Embassy in Colombia for comment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Known for its natural landscapes, vibrant cities and rich culture, Colombia also faces persistent problems with crime, terrorism and violence involving illegal armed groups.

In August, the country was rocked by a deadly 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia, killing at least 289 people and destroying over 26,000 homes.

The disaster came as U.S. officials warned Americans to reconsider travel to the country due to crime, terrorism, civil unrest and kidnapping.

item.title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, Ken Urker, found dead inside his Louisiana home: sheriff
item.description: Ken Urker was found dead in his Louisiana home after loved ones couldn't reach him. Gypsy Rose Blanchard says she believes it was a drug overdose.
item.content:encoded:
The Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office confirmed Kenan "Ken" Urker, the partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, was found dead inside his Louisiana home Thursday after loved ones requested a welfare check.

Anita Blanchard told authorities that she and her husband, who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard's half-brother, went to the 34-year-old's home and spotted Urker lying unconscious from an outside window, according to an incident report.

A man accompanying Anita Blanchard and her husband then entered the house through a window and found Urker, who was not breathing and cold to the touch, according to the report.

GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD IS ENGAGED TO MAN WHO CONTACTED HER IN PRISON, REPORT SAYS

Investigators recovered syringes and a spoon next to a brown powdery substance in the bathroom, as well as a handgun, two shot glasses, and a syringe on a nightstand next to the bed, the report states.

Deputies noted Urker "appeared to have been there for an extended period of time."

Anita Blanchard told authorities that Urker had been with her and her husband at church the previous evening around 8:45 p.m., where he mentioned feeling depressed and upset.

GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD SAYS SHE 'FELT LIKE A PRISONER' BEFORE MOTHER'S FATAL STABBING

"They advised he made a TikTok live video at approximately 2300 hours," deputies wrote. "They advised that he just had the video going while he was driving without him saying anything."

Urker had amassed more than 36,000 followers on the platform.

After Urker failed to show up for work the following day, Anita Blanchard and Urker's employer decided to check on him, ultimately prompting them to contact law enforcement.

The sheriff's office told Fox News Digital the case remains under investigation, but there are "no signs of foul play." Thursday was Urker's 34th birthday.

"If that would change at any point, or there would be any major update in this investigation, we would issue a new statement," the sheriff's office said.

HAYDEN PANETTIERE CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED

Gypsy Rose Blanchard was sentenced to 10 years in prison for second-degree murder in 2016 for her role in the fatal stabbing of her mother, Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard, alongside her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn. The killing inspired the 2019 TV series "The Act" on Hulu.

Godejohn was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Blanchard was released on parole in December 2023 after serving 85% of her sentence.

Urker and Gypsy Rose Blanchard got engaged in 2018 while she was incarcerated, but later separated. The couple rekindled after her first marriage and welcomed their daughter, Aurora, on Dec. 28, 2024.

In a statement to PEOPLE, Blanchard said she believes Urker died of a drug overdose.

"I don’t know if it was intentional or not," Gypsy Rose Blanchard told the outlet. "He was not in a good state of mind lately."

She shared a photo of Urker on Instagram Friday, writing, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever."

Gypsy Rose Blanchard also shared an Instagram Story detailing his struggle with cyberbullying.

"Ken endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit," she wrote. "The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure. I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment."

"I will make sure [Aurora] grows up knowing how deeply her father loved her and who he was beyond what strangers on the internet chose to say about him," she added.

The post, shared with her one million followers, garnered nearly 100,000 likes within hours.

item.title: Social media reacts to excruciatingly awkward moment between Devils Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst
item.description: Jack Hughes' interview with ESPN's AJ Mleczko is already a frontrunner for awkward moment of the year after her injury joke fell completely flat.
item.content:encoded:
The NHL season is just a few days old, and it's safe to say that we have a frontrunner for "Awkward Moment of the Year" already.

This one comes courtesy of New Jersey Devils star Jack Hughes and ESPN analyst AJ Mleczko.

The Devils hosted the Philadelphia Flyers for their season opener at the Prudential Center. After the first period, the Devils were down 1-0, and Hughes was called over to do an interview with Mleczko, who was stationed between the benches.

AVALANCHE FORWARD NATHAN MACKINNON SCORES A PAIR THEN DROPS GLOVES, MIGHT BE THE BEST PLAYER IN THE WORLD

Hughes offered the usual interview platitudes and seemed to be pleased with how his team was playing.

But then Mleczko decided to make a joke about the Team USA golden goal scorer's injury history, including an infamous moment in which he sustained a cut during a team dinner.

WYNDHAM CLARK TROLLS CANADIAN OPEN CROWD WITH TEAM USA JACK HUGHES JERSEY, GETS SHOWERED WITH BOOS

How did it go? Well, about as well as a dog fart at a wake.

Cue the "Curb Your Enthusiasm" music.

It's a rough one, and you've got a clear line of demarcation, with some going after Mleczko for making the joke.

Others said criticism of her was misogynistic or saw it as an opportunity to go after Hughes for laughing at a joke the president made after the gold medal game.

Personally, I think it was a perfect storm of awkwardness. Just an accidental mixing of social bleach and ammonia.

I think Mleczko is a really solid broadcaster, and everyone has moments where they say something they wish they could grab out of the air and pretend it never happened.

Any analyst who tried to make that joke would've ended up with egg on their face too.

Buuuuuuut...

Hughes is not known to be one of the more gregarious NHLers. If you make a joke like that, someone like the Flyers' Trevor Zegras or Florida's Brad Marchand would field it and probably volley one back in the other direction.

I think Mleczko's biggest mistake was taking the wrong approach with the wrong player.

Who cares? Everyone goofs up.

But it is also weird to take an awkward moment, tie it back to an unrelated and overblown moment from months earlier, in a vain attempt to build a narrative that just doesn't seem to be there.

item.title: College football refs ruin another game, Paige Spiranac whips up some eggs & Tony Romo's next move
item.description: First Friday of October brings blown calls in Oklahoma, Lexie Hull's brutal WNBA takedown and Tony Romo's quiet exit from CBS after arrest.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

First Friday of October? Come on! Might be right up there with the best weekend of the year. Fall is in the air. The leaves are turning. The sun is setting just a tad earlier every night. The weather is crisping up nicely.

Unless, of course, you're down here in Florida. It's rained every single day this week. It's raining right now. It'll be raining later. It's horrible.

We actually lost power, briefly, during the Braves game earlier this week. My wife is a huge Braves fan. It was chaos. I thought we were all done for.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Luckily, it came back on a few minutes later. The Braves went on to win. And then they won again last night. That means it's gonna be a much better first October weekend in this house.

Phew.

Let's roll.

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where the college football refs ruined yet another game last night. Amazing.

What else? I've got Paige Spiranac whipping up some breakfast to get our weekend started with a bang, Lexie Hull getting tossed around like a ragdoll while the equally insufferable WNBA refs turned a blind eye and the Tony Romo era at CBS is officially donezo.

But have we heard that last from Tony? I doubt it. You'll see.

OK, grab you whatever you need to get you through the final few hours of this work day, and settle in for a first-Friday-of-October 'Cap!

This is gonna be a quick class, because it's a Friday and we have college football to bet on tonight.

How about Virginia Tech, by the way? The Hokies are 4-0 and now we're getting a meaningful night game in Blacksburg for the first time in what feels like a decade?

Goodness, how lucky are we? Pitt-Va. Tech. at 7 p.m., and we also get Northwestern christening their new stadium against Penn State at 8 p.m. over on Fox. Like I said yesterday — this is the best time of year.

Soak it all in, boys and girls. Don't waste a single second.

OK, now we're gonna start class with last night's debacle in Oklahoma, where Tulsa was screwed out of a game-winning two-point conversion ...

But they also shouldn't have been there in the first place:

Thoughts? First impressions?

In no world is that first "touchdown" a touchdown. It's just simply the incorrect call. I couldn't believe my eyes as I was watching it live. You can't step out and then touch the ball before reestablishing yourself. That's Football 101. It was clear as day, they reviewed it for 20 seconds, and then upheld the call.

Ridiculous. What are we doing here? There has to be some accountability. It's nonsense.

BREAKING UP TROY AIKMAN AND JOE BUCK WOULD BE A BIG MISTAKE FOR ESPN | BOBBY BURACK

As for the non-call in overtime ... that one is a little tougher for me. It's certainly not as clear as the first play.

This angle makes me think it was a conversion:

I don't see a knee on the ground. I don't see a shin on the ground. I don't see a cheek on the ground. I see the ball break the plane.

Again, that one's a tougher call because it's close. The call on the field worked against Tulsa, so I can see them upholding it. Don't agree with it, but I understand the logic behind it.

The first one, though? That's nasty work by the refs. Both teams deserved better last night.

And you know who else deserved better? Lexie Hull, who's spending her first day of the WNBA offseason in an ice bath:

Goodness gracious. Just a violent takedown. And, somehow, the foul is called on the player who is currently getting arm-barred into next week.

The entire sequence is just so perfect for the WNBA. It's everything right — and wrong — with that league.

The officiating is just horrible. That's No. 1. We forget about just how truly awful the officials are most of the year because there's so much other nonsense going on, but at the end of the day, they are undoubtedly the worst officials in all of sports.

And that includes the nonsense we saw in Tulsa last night!

Remember earlier this summer when Sophie Cunningham got her teeth cracked by an elbow and no foul was called? Amazing. Same thing here with Lexie Hull.

Good riddance, WNBA. No, the season isn't over. But nobody will watch or care anymore. Caitlin Clark is out. Sophie Cunningham is out. It's over.

Can't wait to see the girls lace 'em back up next May! All eyes on the draft.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big Friday night. First up? We've ripped college football and WNBA officials so far today ...

Might as well end it with the fellas in the NFL!

This isn't a great look for the "there's no Patrick Mahomes bias in the NFL!" crowd ...

Lordy. I knew it was bad when I watched it live last Sunday. I said as much in Monday's class. But I didn't realize it was that bad.

Now, a couple things ...

Next? On the way out, let's all say goodbye to Tony Romo ... for now:

I'll be the first to admit, I didn't think CBS would do it. When Romo got arrested last summer, I figured he'd be back in the booth in no time.

I believe I even said he'd be back before Game 1. I was wrong.

Things were very clearly bad behind the scenes. So bad, CBS basically bought him out and decided to eat the contract. I'm not a huge Romo fan. I think he's been pretty awful the past few years.

That being said ... I'd be shocked if he doesn't land a pretty big gig next season. I have no clue where it'll be, but I wouldn't bet against him.

Maybe Netflix? They appear to be getting pretty serious about the NFL.

There's also something ... fishy ... going on with Troy Aikman and ESPN at the moment. Joe Buck just signed a massive contract extension with ESPN, but it's been all quiet on the Aikman front. Him and Buck have historically been a package deal.

Maybe it's nothing. But, maybe it's something worth watching.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Happy first weekend of October, everyone. Let's go have a big one.

Take us home, Chef Paige!

Thoughts on the Tulsa game? Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

item.title: Wynonna Judd calls out Rosie O’Donnell after political comments leave country star ‘in shock’
item.description: Wynonna Judd pushed back after longtime friend Rosie O'Donnell labeled her a Trump supporter, calling the claim a "complete assumption."
item.content:encoded:
Wynonna Judd was caught off guard when she learned what Rosie O’Donnell had been saying about her political beliefs.

The country music icon is pushing back after O'Donnell publicly described her as a supporter of President Donald Trump.

"I’m in shock, just so you know," Judd told People. "I’ve never spoken to her about politics in my life. … She doesn’t know anything about my stuff. I’m an independent.

ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS

"I don’t know where it came [from]. It’s complete assumption," she said. "I heard it and I went, ‘What the …?’ I don’t ever remember talking to her about this, so she’s just assuming.’

"I’m not angry," she added, describing herself as confused by O’Donnell’s comments.

But Judd said there was never a political conversation for O’Donnell to draw that conclusion from.

And she isn't interested in turning the misunderstanding into a celebrity political battle.

"I just don’t want drama," Judd said. "So, if there’s going to be drama [about it], I’m like, ‘Oh for crap’s sake, there’s so much going on right now in the world. Can we just love each other?’"

Fox News Digital has reached out to O’Donnell for comment.

Judd's comments come after O’Donnell discussed their friendship during an August appearance on "The Tangle with Kyle Ridley" podcast.

"I kind of give her a grace in a way. She’s had so much in her life, with her mom taking her own life and just the complicated nature of her upbringing. And I really love her, and I care about her. And, for some reason, I’m able to put that aside when we interact."

Her relationship with O’Donnell stretches back decades. Judd was a recurring guest on O’Donnell’s daytime talk show in the 1990s, and the pair have remained friends long after the program ended.

item.title: NFL suspends and fines 49ers owner Jed York for violation of conduct policy tied to prostitution arrest
item.description: Jed York's NFL suspension and $500,000 fine stem from a prostitution sting at a trailer park that left the 49ers owner facing mounting costs.
item.content:encoded:
Going hunting for a prostitute in a trailer park wasn't the smartest thing San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York ever did and the NFL on Friday fined and suspended him for it.

The NFL announced York has been suspended six games and fined $500,000 for violating the league's Personal Conduct Policy. Three games of the suspension have already been served by York.

York released a statement in which he apologized for his "inexcusable mistake."

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

"Today, the NFL concluded its review, and I accept its decision in fully," York said in a statement. "To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry.

"This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one's failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better.

"Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don't take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

York had $160 on his person when he was taken into custody by the East Palestine police department in conjunction with the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force on Aug. 23.

The arrest happened when York allegedly responded to an online prostitution advertisement and upon his arrival at a meeting site that was actually a residential trailer park.

So the NFL's fine and suspension, court costs and other fees, makes this a pretty expensive, not to mention embarrassing, attempt to hire an imaginary sex worker.

York has stayed away from the 49ers since he pleaded no contest to two misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools, meaning his cell phone, which he used to seek out the meeting.

Adding the court fine, the NFL fine, and the $160 seized during the sting and forfeited to the task force, York's total cost will be $501,310.

"During the time the league's investigation has been proceeding, York has stayed away from the 49ers first three regular-season games, as well as from NFL league meetings," the NFL said in a statement.

"Those three missed games are counted toward his suspension, and he may return on Oct. 20."

item.title: Dems demanding Venezuela brief face State Department fury as senators leave town before meeting
item.description: Senate Democrats have challenged the legality of a Pentagon equity stake in Venezuelan oil company NABEP, but the State Department fires back sharply.
item.content:encoded:
The State Department is accusing Democrats of performative "grandstanding" by demanding a sweeping Venezuela oil deal briefing then postponing it so the Senate could leave town early.

Four senior Senate Democrats demanded documents they already knew were coming, according to material reviewed by Fox News Digital. Then, the Senate rescheduled a congressional briefing on the agreement planned for Oct. 1, 2026, so it could break for fall recess.

The group of lawmakers were seeking more information on the Pentagon's involvement in an agreement with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) that gives the Department of War a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers. 

TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES

State says the lawmakers had known for weeks that administration officials planned to brief the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and provide documents on the deal on Thursday.

The department went forward with delivering copies of the U.S. government’s strategic partnership agreement with NABEP to the committee, claiming it did so despite the briefing being pulled down "as a courtesy."

"Copies of the USG Strategic Partnership Agreement with NABEP for your Members are in the SFRC front office," a senior State Department official wrote. "Each Member has a folder with their copy."

State Department Assistant Secretary for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson claimed Senate Democrats canceled the briefing so they could "skip town and go on vacation."

"This is pure grandstanding," Johnson wrote on X. "When they sent this letter, they had known for weeks that we planned to brief them and provide the documents today, on October 1."

A congressional source familiar with the planned briefing disputed State’s characterization, telling Fox News Digital that lawmakers had not been told the written NABEP agreement would be provided before writing the letter and that the briefing was intended as a broader update on U.S. policy toward Venezuela, not specifically the oil deal.

And emails reviewed by Fox News Digital show the briefing postponement request itself came from a Republican majority staffer on the Foreign Relations Committee, who told State early Oct. 1 that "the Senate has left town" and asked to move the briefing until November.

A State Department official told Fox News Digital the staffer was acting on behalf of the full committee.

The congressional source said Republican leadership had ended legislative business for the week, with senators on both sides of the aisle preparing to leave Washington ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

The group of Democrat lawmakers demanding the briefing are challenging the legality and prudence of the Trump administration’s agreement with NABEP, which would give the Pentagon rights to a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers.

Under the arrangement, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital would receive rights to the stake through so-called penny warrants, while the State Department would receive preferential rights to purchase 20% of the company’s production at cost.

The unusual structure is part of the administration’s broader effort to revive Venezuelan oil production and expand U.S. economic influence after Nicolás Maduro’s ouster. Democrats argue the Pentagon may lack legal authority to take the stake and have raised questions about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership.

The administration argues the structure could generate substantial returns for the U.S. without requiring taxpayers to buy the stake up front. The White House has said the government’s 35% position could ultimately be worth hundreds of billions of dollars in equity and dividends if NABEP succeeds in developing the fields.

The deal could also give Washington a new source of relatively low-cost crude at a time when the administration is trying to increase global supply and bring down fuel prices. State would have the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s production at cost and the right of first refusal on the remaining output, which the administration says could help replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and supply U.S. military and other sensitive needs.

The White House also says millions of barrels of additional Venezuelan production could eventually flow through U.S. refineries and be developed using American drilling equipment and infrastructure, generating investment and jobs in the United States.

NABEP produces roughly 220,000 barrels a day and has said it plans to more than double production to 500,000 barrels a day by late 2028. The administration is betting that private investment can revive fields that have suffered years of underinvestment and mismanagement.

The agreement is part of a much broader U.S. effort to remake Venezuela’s economy after the dramatic removal of Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

On Jan. 3, U.S. forces carried out a military operation in Venezuela to capture Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and transport them to the United States to face federal charges. The administration has characterized the operation as a law enforcement mission supported by the military and has since made rebuilding Venezuela’s oil sector a central part of its stabilization strategy.

Interim leader Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s former vice president, has remained in power while cooperating with Washington, even as Venezuela’s political transition remains unsettled and opposition figures continue pressing for elections.

The White House has described the NABEP agreement as part of a three-part strategy of stabilization, reconstruction and eventual democratic transition, arguing that restoring oil production is necessary to rebuild Venezuela’s economy and reduce the influence of China, Russia and other U.S. adversaries in its energy sector.

TRUMP 'SERIOUSLY CONSIDERING' PLAN TO MAKE VENEZUELA AND ITS $40 TRILLION IN OIL PERMANENT PART OF USA

Senators Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H.; Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., challenged both the legality and prudence of the deal in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

Among their central questions is whether the Pentagon office being used to structure the investment has the legal authority to acquire an equity position in a foreign oil company. The senators also demanded the agreement itself, details about how State would pay for oil and information about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership.

"The proposed agreement is unlikely to reduce high energy costs for Americans, and it risks undermining the Venezuelan people’s transition away from a dictatorship," the senators wrote.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of all four senators who signed the letter for comment.

The unusual Pentagon role has drawn scrutiny since the deal was announced. Rather than immediately purchasing shares with taxpayer money, the Office of Strategic Capital’s position is structured through penny warrants that give the government the right to acquire equity for a nominal price.

The Democratic senators argue that structure does not resolve the underlying legal question.

They contend the statute establishing the Office of Strategic Capital authorizes loans and loan guarantees but does not explicitly empower the Pentagon to acquire equity stakes in private foreign companies.

"It is unclear," the lawmakers wrote, "why the American public should support this attempt to entangle the United States with a relatively unknown foreign oil company that lacks the capacity or credibility to develop oil fields of the magnitude described."

The senators also raised concerns about NABEP Chairman Alejandro Betancourt, noting past money-laundering investigations involving the Venezuelan businessman. Betancourt has not been charged with a crime, and Rubio has previously said he is not under active U.S. investigation.

The dispute could form the basis for broader congressional scrutiny of one of the Trump administration’s most unconventional efforts to expand U.S. economic influence in Venezuela.

item.title: Android malware can steal your PIN and bank logins
item.description: RatHat Android malware uses AI to steal banking credentials, intercept two-factor authentication codes and reconstruct your PIN from touch inputs.
item.content:encoded:
Your Android phone probably holds far more sensitive information than you realize. Banking apps, passwords and security codes can all pass through that little screen in your hand. A newly uncovered Android threat called RatHat wants access to all of it.

Security researchers at Zimperium discovered the malware, which uses generative AI as part of its attack, and found that it can turn permissions you approve into surprisingly deep control of your phone. RatHat can steal banking credentials, intercept authentication codes and even reconstruct a PIN or unlock pattern from where your finger touches the screen. It can also create a persistent connection that may survive after you remove the malicious app.

The attack still needs help from the person holding the phone. RatHat relies heavily on tricking someone into installing a malicious Android app and approving powerful permissions. That gives you several opportunities to stop it before the malware takes over.

AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

RatHat starts with social engineering. Zimperium says attackers primarily spread it through SMS phishing, malicious advertising and deceptive third-party download sites. The malicious APK may pose as familiar software, including a streaming app or Chrome. 

That familiar name can lower your guard. A download page might look convincing enough to make you think you are installing a normal app. However, RatHat relies on you manually installing an APK outside Google Play. Once installed, the malicious app pushes you to enable Android's Accessibility service. 

The excuse can vary by region. In some cases, the malware claims the permission will solve a network problem or unlock a financial benefit. Accessibility services perform important legitimate functions on Android. However, they can also give an approved app the ability to inspect what appears on your screen and interact with the interface. RatHat takes advantage of that power to begin changing settings without you doing the work yourself.

Once RatHat gets Accessibility access, it can tap through Android settings to enable Developer Options and Wireless Debugging. It can then read the six-digit ADB pairing code displayed on the phone and connect to the device's own Android Debug Bridge. No separate computer has to complete the connection. ADB, short for Android Debug Bridge, gives developers powerful tools to test and manage Android devices. 

RatHat abuses that legitimate feature to establish shell-level access outside the normal Android app sandbox. From there, the malware launches a Go-based agent that can execute system commands. It also starts a reverse-proxy client that creates a persistent connection back to the attacker. Zimperium says that connection can give an operator continued access to the phone's ADB service. RatHat also brings AI into the process. 

The malware sends information from Android's live Accessibility tree to a generative AI assistant. The AI can help determine where an item appears on the screen, read displayed text and tell the malware when to scroll. That makes the attack more adaptable than automation that follows the same fixed sequence every time. We recently saw another Android threat abuse Wireless Debugging in a similar way. RatHat adds AI-assisted navigation and another persistence mechanism to the mix.

After gaining access, RatHat can watch for financial apps and display fake screens over legitimate ones. Those overlays can trick you into entering banking credentials directly into a page controlled by the attacker. Zimperium found RatHat targeting banking and cryptocurrency apps. 

It also specifically identified overlays aimed at payment services such as WeChat and Alipay. The malware can intercept SMS messages and notification content as well, giving attackers another way to capture one-time passwords and two-factor authentication codes. Then there is the way RatHat watches your fingers. The malware can monitor raw touch coordinates and compare those locations with known keypad layouts. That allows it to reconstruct PINs from where you tap. 

It can use a similar method to recover Android pattern-lock sequences. Because the malware reads those touch coordinates at a low level, protections that normally hide PIN digits from screen readers do not stop this technique. That means a criminal may never need to see your PIN displayed as text. Your finger movements can give it away.

RatHat also tries to make leaving your phone much harder than getting onto it. Zimperium found that the malware can interfere when you try to uninstall the malicious app. It can cancel the real uninstall process and place a fake Google Play error message on top of the screen. Even if you successfully remove the visible app, another problem remains. RatHat launches a separate native service outside the normal app life cycle. 

That service can stay behind after the original app disappears. It can then reinstall the malware and restore its permissions. Zimperium also found that RatHat can request Device Admin rights. Those rights give it additional control, including the ability to wipe the device if someone tries to uninstall it. That persistence is why deleting a suspicious app may not be enough once RatHat fully compromises a phone.

Google responded to CyberGuy and says it has not found RatHat on Google Play based on its current detection. The company also says Android users already have protection against known versions of the malware through Google Play Protect. 

"Based on our current detection, no apps containing this malware are found on Google Play. Android users are automatically protected against known versions of this malware by Google Play Protect, which is on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy. 

That is reassuring for people who download their apps through Google Play. It also reinforces why keeping Play Protect enabled can add an important layer of defense if a harmful app reaches your phone from another source.

RatHat becomes dangerous after it gains several layers of access. Fortunately, you can break that chain at several points. These steps can reduce your risk and help you respond if something has already gone wrong.

HACKERS HIJACK VERIFIED STREAMING ACCOUNT TO SPREAD MALWARE, RESEARCHERS FIND

Avoid installing APK files that arrive through text messages, online ads or unfamiliar websites. RatHat relies heavily on persuading people to sideload malicious apps. If a page looks like Google Play, but you can see a browser address bar, you are still on a website. Close it and open the actual Google Play Store app. Also question any message that tells you to reinstall Chrome or another app already on your phone. Open Google Play yourself and check the app there instead.

Accessibility access plays a central role in RatHat's attack. Therefore, treat an unexpected request for that permission as a serious warning. Open Settings and search for Accessibility. Review apps with Accessibility access and remove permission from anything you do not recognize or no longer use. Menu names can vary by Android phone. If a streaming app, browser update or other unrelated app suddenly tells you that Accessibility access is required, do not approve it until you know exactly why.

Most Android users never need Wireless Debugging. RatHat uses it to establish its powerful ADB shell connection. Open Settings and search for Developer options or Wireless debugging. Leave Wireless Debugging turned off unless you have a specific reason to use it. If you discover Developer Options or Wireless Debugging enabled and you do not remember turning them on, take a closer look at the apps and security settings on your phone.

Install strong antivirus software and keep real-time protection enabled. Security software can help detect malicious apps and suspicious activity before they get deeper access to your phone. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

However, detecting RatHat and completely removing it are two different things. Because the malware can leave behind a persistent service after the visible app is removed, we recommend a factory reset if a security scan confirms RatHat has fully infected your phone.

Google says Android users are automatically protected against known versions of RatHat through Google Play Protect, which comes turned on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. You can still check that it is enabled. Open the Google Play Store > tap your profile picture > Play Protect > Settings. Make sure Scan apps with Play Protect is turned on. You can also enable Improve harmful app detection. This gives Google additional information about unfamiliar apps installed outside Google Play so they can be checked for harmful behavior.

Android's Advanced Protection can provide another useful barrier on supported devices. Google says it blocks app installations from unknown sources and restricts Accessibility services to verified accessibility tools. It also prevents Play Protect from being turned off while Device protection is active. To turn it on, open Settings > Security & privacy > Advanced Protection > turn on Device protection. Google notes that your phone may need to restart. For someone who rarely sideloads apps, those extra restrictions can remove two of the avenues RatHat relies on.

THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE

Install Android security updates and app updates when they become available. Updates fix known vulnerabilities and strengthen protections across your phone. RatHat's documented infection chain depends primarily on malicious downloads and permission abuse, so an Android update alone will not solve the problem. Even so, running current software closes other security gaps that attackers could try to exploit.

RatHat spreads partly through smishing, which is phishing delivered by text message. An urgent message can push you toward a malicious download before you stop to question it. Avoid tapping links in unexpected texts that tell you to install an app or fix a problem on your phone. Instead, open the company's official app or visit its known website yourself. The same advice applies to online ads offering apps. Malvertising can lead to convincing download pages that have nothing to do with the company they appear to represent.

If antivirus software flags RatHat or you have strong reason to think your phone has been compromised, stop entering passwords and financial information on it. Use another trusted device to change important passwords. Start with your primary email account since access to email can help an attacker reset other accounts. Then check your bank and credit card accounts for activity you do not recognize. If you spot anything suspicious, contact the financial institution using the number on the back of your card or through its official app.

If RatHat is confirmed, we recommend a factory reset rather than relying on a normal uninstall. RatHat's separate background component can survive after the visible malicious app disappears. Before resetting the phone, preserve personal photos or documents you know are safe. After the reset, install apps again through Google Play. Avoid reinstalling unfamiliar APK files from an old backup. You should also change credentials from another trusted device before returning to sensitive accounts on the reset phone.

RatHat can target banking credentials and authentication codes, so cleaning the phone should not be the end of your response. Continue reviewing bank statements and login alerts. Also watch for password reset messages or authentication requests you did not initiate. If you believe personal information beyond your login credentials may have been exposed, consider an identity theft protection service that can help monitor for suspicious activity. Acting quickly can limit the damage if stolen information gets used later.

The AI component makes RatHat unusual, but the attack still begins with something very familiar: getting someone to trust the wrong download and approve a powerful permission. That gives Android users a chance to stop RatHat before it reaches the most damaging stages. Google's response adds another important piece of reassurance. The company says no apps containing RatHat are showing up on Google Play based on its detection, and Play Protect already guards Android users against known versions of the malware. 

Still, that protection works best when you avoid sideloading questionable apps and pay close attention to powerful permission requests. Keep Play Protect running and add strong antivirus protection to your phone. Wireless Debugging should stay off unless you know exactly why you need it. If RatHat does make it onto a device, do not assume deleting the app solves the problem. A confirmed infection calls for a much more serious cleanup.

Does knowing AI-powered malware like RatHat can quietly take control of your phone make you think twice about installing apps outside Google Play? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.description: Seth Meyers and John Oliver told Jimmy Kimmel he's their "bulletproof vest" against President Donald Trump, saying he draws all of the president's ire on late night.
item.content:encoded:
Late-night hosts Seth Meyers and John Oliver told Jimmy Kimmel, host of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," on Thursday that he was their "bulletproof vest" when it comes to President Donald Trump.

Oliver said that Kimmel comes up a lot during the question-and-answer portion of stand-up comedy shows he does alongside Meyers.

"Because they’ll normally say, like, how does it feel being, you know, disliked by the current president? And we always say as long as you’re on the air, we’re fine," Oliver said.

"You draw all the ire," Meyers said.

ROBERT DE NIRO JOKINGLY PRODS JIMMY KIMMEL WITH A BASEBALL BAT WHILE POSING AS FCC CHAIR, THREATENS HOST

"We are fully supportive," Oliver told Kimmel. "We are fully behind you the way that we’re fully behind a bulletproof vest."

The group went on to speculate about why Kimmel drew the most attention from the president, and Meyers said, "Other than the fact that you don't like him, we think he would want to hang out with you. "

"I think he sees us as a couple of dorks, and even if we were fans of his, he would have no respect for us. But like, I'm sure he talks to people all the time about like, 'Yeah, I think he has a pizza oven.' Like, everything about, you know what I mean? He's heard you hang out with like, 'You know, he knows Larry David and Conan, he's got a lot of famous friends. His parties sound awesome,'" Meyers said, imitating Trump.

Kimmel said the president never seemed to get upset with Jon Stewart, and noted that he does get upset with Meyers from time to time. He speculated that the president primarily watched the major networks and didn't have HBO, which carries Oliver's show.

"He definitely doesn't have Comedy Central. He has no idea, like most people, no idea where to find that," Kimmel said.

HOWARD STERN WARNS ABC WILL HAVE 'HELL TO PAY' IF SOMETHING 'GOES WRONG' WITH JIMMY KIMMEL'S SHOW

Kimmel told Meyers, "I also think, just as late as he stays up, raging and tweeting and whatever it is he does, you're on too late for him. I think you are past his bedtime."

"I will say that when he posts about my show, it is always when it's airing, and it means the world to me. And I don't love that, but like that he's watching linear television with the ads is so important," Meyers said.

When asked for comment by Fox News Digital, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle called out all three late-night personalities.

"Seriously, unfunny Marble Mouth Meyers might be the dumbest and least talented television host in history. He clearly suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain," Ingle told Fox News Digital.

JIMMY KIMMEL RETURNS FROM LENGTHY HIATUS WITH DEFIANT MESSAGE TO FCC CHAIR BRENDAN CARR

The White House also called out Oliver in a statement and said, "John Oliver is a pathetic moron with a poorly rated TV show."

They pointed Fox News Digital to a previous statement the White House made about Kimmel.

"Jimmy Kimmel is a no-talent loser who has beclowned himself with tanking ratings and by spewing disgusting lies to his dwindling audience. He is so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any commonsense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at his miserable failures," the statement read.

item.title: Florida Gators, Georgia Bulldogs caught in social media standoff over origins of 'Bloody Tuesday' practice
item.description: Jon Sumrall's "Bloody Tuesday" practice ritual sparked a heated debate between Florida Gators and Georgia Bulldogs fans over who coined it first.
item.content:encoded:
Things could not be going much better for the Florida Gators to start the Jon Sumrall era.

Sumrall and his team are 4-0 with a 24-point beatdown of a top-five Ole Miss team less than one week ago.

Recruiting is on fire and the whole program looks like a completely different monster than they did this time a year ago.

FLORIDA DROPS IMPRESSIVE OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE TO PULL OFF MASSIVE WIN OVER NO. 4 OLE MISS

A lot of that is due to Sumrall's intensity as a head coach.

The 44-year-old first-time SEC coach has taken great pride in returning the edge that has been missing from Gainesville since Urban Meyer exited Alachua County back in December 2010.

Just hearing the man talk for more than 60 seconds confirms this, and in keeping with the theme of being an absolute psychopath (in the best way possible, of course), Sumrall is instituting a ritual for his Tuesday practices which will ensure maximum violence and physicality.

He's calling it "Bloody Tuesday."

FLORIDA COACH JON SUMRALL REVEALS EARLY CAREER STRUGGLES, LIVING IN SLUMS OF SAN DIEGO AND 'CARRYING A GLOCK'

"We got a great indoor (practice facility) here," Sumrall said on The Triple Option Podcast. "On Tuesdays, we don’t use the damn indoor. I don’t want anybody going in the indoor on Tuesday. We’re going to be outside. I hope it’s hot. Tuesdays have to be physical and violent, and you gotta strain, or you don’t know how to play way on Saturday."

If you're a Gator fan, you have to be pumped hearing that.

After years and years of milquetoast scrimmages run by mealy mouthed head coaches, it's refreshing to see Sumrall bringing some much-needed juice back to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium.

But not everyone is impressed with Sumrall's "Bloody Tuesday," particularly fans of Florida's archrivals, the Georgia Bulldogs.

Dawg fans on social media have pointed out that Kirby Smart has been using the term "Bloody Tuesday" to describe his weekday practices since arriving in Athens in 2016.

HIGH STAKES, SOCIAL MEDIA BARBS REMIND COLLEGE FOOTBALL FANS THAT AUBURN AND FLORIDA SHARE HISTORY OF HATRED

Uh-oh!

Is Sumrall guilty of copying Kirby's homework and turning it in as his own?

Well, it's a little more complicated than that.

As Gator fans were quick to point out, the aforementioned Urban Meyer started calling his Tuesday practices "Bloody Tuesday" all the way back in 2009, and it perhaps dates back to an even earlier period in the Meyer era.

Georgia fans responded with articles from 2003 showing that former head coach Mark Richt used the phrase early in his tenure, creating a good old fashioned social media standoff.

So who's right here?

The truth of the matter is, both of these fanbases are wasting their breath.

The term "Bloody Tuesday" isn't some revelatory concept; it's literally an adjective followed by a day of the week.

None of these coaches invented the printing press or discovered penicillin, and if you really want to get historical, Richt wasn't even the first one to start using the term "Bloody Tuesday."

Not by a long shot.

A quick Google search shows that legendary Penn State coach Hugo Bezdek coined the phrase back in the 1920s to describe his physical weekday practices with the Nittany Lions.

So, if anyone has a right to be upset with both of these programs, it's the Penn State faithful, though I doubt any of those fans who were alive for Bezdek's reign have an X account to be able to weigh in.

Much of coaching football is taking ideas from your predecessors and adopting them as your own with a personal twist.

Sumrall likely got the idea from Meyer, and Smart likely got the idea from Richt, who in turn adopted it from legendary Georgia coach Vince Dooley.

It's like getting mad at Metallica for using power chords because Black Sabbath did it first.

There's plenty of productive things to argue about between these two fanbases, and "Bloody Tuesday" is pretty far down the list.

Then again, this is part of what makes college football rivalries so great.

Hopefully at their press conferences next week, both Sumrall and Smart pay homage to the true originator of "Bloody Tuesday" so we can all just move on with our lives.

It's the right thing to do.

item.title: Murdaugh lawyers allege prosecutors withheld witness claim that police chief handled murder weapons: filing
item.description: Alex Murdaugh's defense claims prosecutors withheld a witness statement alleging a police chief handled the murder weapons after the 2021 killings.
item.content:encoded:
Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh accused prosecutors Wednesday of withholding a witness statement alleging a South Carolina police chief handled the weapons used to kill Murdaugh's wife and son and arranged a change of clothes for him after the 2021 killings. And they're asking a judge to intervene.

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County.

The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury. His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027.

The new allegations come as Murdaugh's team said "all urgent evidentiary issues" in the case will be heard at a hearing on Oct. 16.

ALEX MURDAUGH DEMANDS NEW EVIDENCE SEARCH IN HUNT FOR CRACKS IN CASE

A spokeswoman for Murdaugh's defense team told Fox News Digital that Judge Debra McCaslin notified them that "DNA, cell phone extraction, ballistic data, and FARO scan data will be addressed at the hearing." 

All other motions will be heard at a Nov. 13 hearing.

The motion, filed by Murdaugh's attorneys Wednesday, cites press reports that a state grand jury heard testimony alleging Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander was seen with the murder weapons shortly after the June 7, 2021, killings.

"According to those reports, witnesses have testified that the Chief of Police of the Town of Yemassee, Greg Alexander, was seen with the murder weapons in the immediate aftermath of the June 7, 2021, killings, and that second Yemassee officer is under investigation for transporting and concealing weapons and clothing," the filing states.

It also cites a story from The Post and Courier, which reported that "a Lowcountry official told SLED agents that Chief Alexander 'spoke of arriving early to the murder scene and talked about providing a change of clothes to Murdaugh,' and that the official believed the guns and clothing were brought into the police station and stored there."

MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS DETECTIVES FOUND MALE DNA UNDER VICTIM'S NAILS BUT SKIPPED KEY TESTING

Notably, the allegations couldn't be corroborated by The Post and Courier.

At Murdaugh's first murder trial in 2023, prosecutors contended that he killed his family members using two different types of weapons, then used a nearby water hose to clean up, changed his clothes and drove to his parents' house, where he allegedly left the murder weapons before returning a week later to dispose of them. Prosecutors had previously acknowledged that police never recovered the weapons.

Alexander, through his attorney, Joe McCulloch, denied accusations made in the media reports. Fox News Digital reached out to Alexander and McCulloch.

Murdaugh's defense team asked a judge to force prosecutors to turn over information it has "concerning the handling, transport, concealment, or disposal of the alleged weapons used to kill Maggie Murdaugh and Paul Murdaugh, including the statement a witness gave to agents of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division in 2023 that a Lowcountry police chief spoke of arriving early at the scene and of providing Defendant Murdaugh a change of clothes, the reports of every interview conducted on that subject, and the testimony and exhibits presented to the State Grand Jury concerning it."

His attorneys said "if the reports are accurate," prosecutors have held evidence that contradicts their own theory.
